sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Aias** (*ajax*) ​— Warrior, ‌Bulwark of ‌Achaeans · ​Of the ​earth — ​belongs to ​the Greek ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Warrior, Bulwark ​of Achaeans". ‌The name ​means "Of ‌the earth"[^1].

​**Aias** is ​the great ​defensive warrior ​of the ​Greek army ‌at Troy. ​In the ‌*Iliad* he ​is second ‌only to ​Achilles in ‌strength and ​courage, a tower ‌of bronze ​and stubbornness ​who saves ‌the Greek ‌ships from ‌fire, duels ​Hector to ​a standstill, ‌and carries ​the dead ​Achilles from ‌the field. ​Where Achilles ​is speed ‌and wrath, ​Aias is ‌mass, endurance, ​and absolute ​loyalty. His ​name became ​a byword ‌for the ‌soldier who ​holds the ‌line when ​everything else ​breaks.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Aias** and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/ajax/). The ​original carries ​both stress ​and vowel ‌length, and ​exactly one ​historically valid ​Unicode restoration ‌exists, which ​places the ​name in ​Tier 1. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*ajax* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Greek ​as ​**Αἴας**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"Of ​the ​earth"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*ajax* ​survives ‌only ​because the ​early ​domain-name ​system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ‌**Aias** ‌recovers ​the ​full diacritic ‌detail ​of ​the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address ‌bar. The ​original ​carries ​both ​stress ‌and vowel ‌length, ​and ‌exactly ​one ​historically valid ‌Unicode ‌restoration ‌exists, ‌which ​places the ‌name ​in ​Tier ​1.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

​- ‌**a** ​→ **A** ​— ​Same
‌- ​**j** ‌→ **i** ​— ‌Iota
​- ‌**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ​Same
​- ​**x** ‌→ **s** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/aí̯.aːs/** ​— Attic ​Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

‌- **Ai-** ​— Long ​diphthong αι ‌[ai̯] carrying ​the ‌acute pitch ​accent; the ‌alpha is ​open ​and the ​iota forms ​an off-glide.
​- ‌**-as** — ​Long alpha ‌[aː] followed ​by ‌voiceless sibilant ​[s], the ‌nominal ending ​of ‌the hero's ​name.

For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ‌closest ‌approximation is: ​'AH-yahs' — ​the first ‌syllable ​is long ​and carries ‌the ancient ​pitch ​rise; the ‌final syllable ​is open ‌and ​sustained.

Kindred ​and historical ​forms of ​the ‌name:

- ‌**Greek** — ​Αἴας (Aias), ‌the ​bulwark of ​the Achaeans ‌in the ‌Iliad
- ‌**Latin** ‌— Ajax, ​the Roman ‌rendering adopted ​into ​English and ​many modern ‌languages

The ​Greek ​Αἴας contains ​both stress ‌(acute on ​the ​diphthong) and ​length (long ‌alpha in ​the ‌diphthong and ​final syllable), ‌making it ​a Tier ‌1 ‌restoration. The ​Latin-derived English ​form Ajax ​is ​a secondary ‌spelling, not ‌the original ​Greek.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌written ‌in ​Greek as ​**Αἴας**. ​This ​original script ​is ‌the ​form against ​which ‌the ​ASCII fallback ‌*ajax* ​and ‌the PuniCodex ​restoration ​**Aias** are ​measured: ​the ​restoration preserves ‌its ​full ‌diacritic detail ​of ‌the ​written form, ‌so ​that ‌a reader ​typing ​the ‌modern address ‌still ‌speaks the ​ancient ​name.[^1]

‌The name ​is ​written ‌in Greek ​as ​**Αἴας**. ‌The first ​syllable ‌is ​a long ​diphthong ​αι ​with an ‌acute ‌accent; ​the final ‌alpha ​is long. ​The ‌Latin ‌form *Ajax* ‌and ‌English ​*Ajax* are ‌secondary ​spellings ​that mask ​the ‌original ​Greek vowel ​quantities. ​The ‌PuniCodex restoration ​**Aias** ​recovers the ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ‌Greek ​form ‌and is ​classified ‌as ‌Tier 1 ​because ​both ​pitch accent ​and ‌vowel ‌length are ​preserved.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Aias** ​is the ‌great defensive ‌warrior of ​the Greek ​army ​at Troy. ​In the ​*Iliad* he ‌is second ​only to ​Achilles ‌in strength ​and courage, ‌a tower ​of bronze ‌and ​stubbornness who ​saves the ​Greek ships ​from fire, ​duels Hector ‌to ​a standstill, ‌and carries ​the dead ‌Achilles from ​the ‌field. Where ​Achilles is ‌speed and ​wrath, Aias ​is mass, ‌endurance, ‌and absolute ‌loyalty. His ​name became ​a byword ‌for ​the soldier ​who holds ‌the line ​when everything ​else breaks.[^1]

‌### ​The Shield ‌Wall

Aias ​fights with ​a towering ​seven-fold ​oxhide shield ‌that protects ‌whole companies, ​not merely ‌himself.

### ​Duel ​with Hector

‌He meets ‌Hector in ‌single combat ‌and ​fights him ‌to a ​draw, proving ​that defence ​can match ‌offence.

​### Rescue ​of Achilles

​After Patroclus ‌falls, Aias ​stands ​over the ​body and ‌bears Achilles' ​corpse from ‌the battlefield.

​### ‌Tragic Pride

​Denied Achilles' ‌armour, he ‌falls into ​a ​madness of ​shame and ​takes his ‌own life ‌on the ​seashore.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Aias ​concentrates in ​a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement about ‌the ​name:[^1]

​- ​**Seven-fold ​oxhide ​shield** ‌— ​The ‌massive tower-shield ​that ‌makes ​Aias ‌a ​living ‌fortress ​and ​protects ‌the ‌whole Greek ‌line.
​- ​**Sword** ‌— ​The ​weapon ‌with ​which ​he ‌slays sheep ​in ‌his ​madness ​and ​then ​himself ‌in ‌the ​tragedy ‌of Sophocles.
​- ​**The ‌ships** ‌— ‌The ‌beached ​Greek ‌fleet ​that ​Aias defends ​when ‌the ​Trojans ​press ​it ‌with ​fire.
​- ​**The seashore** ‌— ​The ‌place ​of ‌his ​suicide ‌and ‌burial, ​where ​the waves ​meet ​the ‌land ‌of ​Troy.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The myths ​of Aias are told ‌in the *Iliad*, ‌the lost Epic ​Cycle, and above all ​in Sophocles' tragedy ​*Aias*. They turn on ​a single quality: ​the absolute, unbending ‌commitment of the warrior. ​That quality makes ​him the Greeks' ‌greatest defender and, when ​it is slighted, ‌their most terrible casualty.[^1]

​### The Defence ‌of the Ships ​(Iliad)

When the Trojans ​break through to ​the Greek ships and ​set a ship ​ablaze, Aias holds ‌the line alone. He ​plants himself on ‌the decks with ​his great shield and ‌drives back the ​attackers while the Greeks ‌rally behind him. ​Homer compares him ‌to a donkey that ​children cannot move ​from a cornfield: ugly ‌to mock, impossible ‌to shift.[^2]

### ‌Duel with Hector (Iliad)

​After Hector challenges ​the Greeks to ‌single combat, Aias is ​chosen by lot. ​The two champions fight ‌until nightfall, exchanging ​blows so heavy ​that the earth shakes. ‌Neither wins; they ​exchange gifts and part ‌with mutual respect. ​It is the ​closest the *Iliad* comes ​to showing Hector ​matched by equal honour.

‌### The Rescue ‌of Achilles' Body ​(Epic Cycle)

When Achilles ‌is killed by ​Paris and Apollo ​at the Scaean Gate, ‌Aias and Odysseus ‌fight through the Trojans ‌to recover the ‌corpse. Aias lifts ​the body onto his ‌shoulders and carries ​it from the field ​while Odysseus drives ​off the attackers. ‌The rescue proves Aias' ​strength and his ​devotion to his ​comrades.

### The Madness ‌and Suicide (Sophocles)

​After Achilles' death, the ​Greeks award his ​armour to Odysseus ‌rather than Aias. Maddened ​by Athena, Aias ‌attacks a flock of ​sheep believing them ‌to be his ​enemies. When he returns ‌to sanity and ‌sees what he ​has done, shame overwhelms ​him. He falls ​on his sword, and ​the debate over ‌whether to bury ‌him honourably divides the ​Greek commanders.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Aias ​was ‌honoured ‌as ​a hero ​at ​Salamis, ​his ​father's ‌island, ​and ​at Athens, ‌where ​the ‌festival ​Aianteia ‌included ​games ​in his ​honour. ​The ​Athenians ‌claimed ​him ‌as ​their ‌own through ​his ‌father ​Telamon's ‌exile ​there. ​Roman ‌writers such ‌as ‌Ovid ​retold ​his ‌story, ​and ​the name ‌Ajax ​passed ​into ‌modern ​culture ‌as ​a ​byword for ​physical ​might ‌and ‌tragic ​pride. ‌In ​the twentieth ​century ‌it ‌became ‌a ‌brand ​name ‌for cleaning ​products ​and ​football ‌clubs, ​a ​long ​descent ‌from the ​Homeric ​bulwark.[^1]

​Within ‌the ​Greek ‌tradition, ​closely related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], ​[[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], ​[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aither|Aithḗr]], ‌and ​[[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is yet ​assigned ​to ‌Aias ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence should ​be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek name ​of ‌this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record is ​expected ‌to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary evidence ​remains ​the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in the ​Scholarly ​Sources ‌section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ​would ‌take ‌recognizable ​forms: votive ‌or ​dedicatory ​inscriptions ‌naming ‌Αἴας, ‌sanctuary ‌or cult ​remains ‌tied ​to ​warrior ​and ‌iconography matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(seven-fold ​oxhide ​shield and ​sword). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Aias ​teaches ‌that ‌strength ​without flexibility ​can ​become ​its ​own ‌enemy. ​His ​refusal ‌to bend ​before ‌the ​Greek ‌commanders ​is ​the ​same ​refusal that ​let ‌him ​hold ‌the ​ships ‌against ​Hector; ‌turned inward, ​it ‌becomes ​the ​sword ‌with ‌which ‌he ​destroys himself. ​The ‌modern ​reader ​cannot ‌easily ​judge ​him. ‌His suicide ​is ‌at ​once ​a ​failure ​of ‌proportion ‌and a ​terrible ‌assertion ​of ​dignity.

‌To ‌remember ‌Aias ‌is to ​remember ‌the ​cost ​of ​asking ‌human ​beings ​to be ​shields. ‌The ​wall ​that ​protects ‌others ​must ‌itself bear ​every ‌blow. ​When ‌the ‌wall ​is ​slighted, ​the whole ​structure ‌of ‌honour ​trembles.[^1]
